items.title: Avengers: Doomsday has brought with it more ‘Marvel homework’ than ever. That’s just as it should be
items.summary:
Working out where returning hero Steve Rogers has been is only one of the multiversal puzzles fans must now get their heads around – which is catnip for the connoisseurs

The cinema release of Avengers: Doomsday is now roughly three weeks away and, judging by the final trailer, we’re living in the one timeline where every loose end Marvel has left dangling for years is now worth tugging on. Even the ones we thought the studio had tied up rather nicely. Ever since it became apparent that Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers would be returning in the new film, along with next year’s sequel Avengers: Secret Wars, fans have been asking themselves: where exactly has he been all this time? Now, thanks to the latest footage, we’re beginning to get an idea, and we might also be starting to pick up clues as to why Doctor Doom would take an interest in his new postcode.

One of the most startling aspects of the new trailer is the arrival of the Fantastic Four, led by Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards, on Rogers’ front lawn. We’ve known since the finale of Avengers: Endgame that Steve used Tony Stark’s newly discovered time-travelling tech to go back to the 1940s and live out his life with Peggy Carter during the events of that film – but until recently it seemed most likely that happened in good old Earth-616, the main Marvel Cinematic Universe continuity.
items.t: Avengers: Doomsday has brought with it more ‘Marvel homework’ than ever. That’s just as it should be

items.title: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas
items.summary:
The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist

“With the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on the Lifetime reality show Dance Moms in 2011, before becoming the unlikely muse of the publicity-shy singer Sia, which led to a role in Steven Spielberg’s West Side Story. Ziegler’s latest project is In a Holidaze, a fuzzy Christmas movie that comes to Netflix on 2 December. “I’ve actually never done a romcom before,” she says, speaking on a recent Zoom call from Los Angeles. “I grew up loving Christmas movies so much, so when this came into my lap, I was so excited.’”

In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually revolve around romance and family, with an aesthetic quality and winking irony that feels similar to Hallmark – the American card-maker turned movie giant, whose very name is synonymous with cliches.
items.t: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas

items.title: ‘Everybody tells me how I can keep working. My answer begins with ‘F’ and ends with ‘off’: Mike Leigh on 55 years of films – and why he’s just made his last
items.summary:
The acclaimed director has announced his latest film Tender Loving Care will be his last. He talks about coming to terms with a life-changing condition and how he would have loved to have made a big budget modern-day movie

Mike Leigh and his partner, the actor Marion Bailey, were knocking around at home last Christmas, looking for a good film to watch and constantly coming up short. Finally, Leigh had a brilliant idea. Why not put on Topsy-Turvy, his 1999 costume romp about the making of The Mikado? Problem solved, perfect choice. “It’s not like a habit,” he says hurriedly. “I don’t sit there watching my films every night like Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard. It’s just that Topsy-Turvy happens to be a very enjoyable watch.”

The way Leigh sees it, his films are like children. They’ve outgrown him, moved on, but it’s nice to check the family ties are still strong. Some are sunny (Life is Sweet; Happy-Go-Lucky) and some are dour (Naked; Hard Truths), but they all share the same DNA, the same real-world interests and tragicomic mindset. He can’t choose between them; he’ll defend each one to the death. Then he pauses and says, “But I’ve got a soft spot for Meantime.”

Continue reading...

items.title: You Can See Everything overtly riffs on Vertigo. But how big is its debt to Kiarostami’s Close-Up?
items.summary:
The Iranian film-maker’s 1990 tale of impersonation and deception happens to be a favourite movie of the Elizabeth Holmes docufiction’s co-director Lance Oppenheim
• NB: This article contains spoilers

You’re probably sick of hearing how You Can See Everything, about the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, is the buzziest, coolest, 100% freshest film of the year, but coming out of the screening last week, I couldn’t help but wonder whether Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim had been watching a lot of 90s Iranian cinema. And one film in particular: Close-Up, by Abbas Kiarostami.

If it feels as if You Can See Everything blends truth, lies, fiction and documentary in mind-bending new ways until you’re no longer sure what the hell you’re watching, then Kiarostami, who died in 2016, practically invented this mode 36 years ago. The context could not be more different – analogue 90s Tehran rather than tech-drunk 2020s California – but the themes are the same: Close-Up is a strange story of impersonation, deception and performance, made even stranger by the film-maker’s deliberate meddling.

Continue reading...
items.t: You Can See Everything overtly riffs on Vertigo. But how big is its debt to Kiarostami’s Close-Up?

items.title: You Can See Everything passes $100m at global box office as UK release starts strong
items.summary:
The documentary from Nathan Fielder following fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment has broken box office records in the UK

Elizabeth Holmes film You Can See Everything has crossed the $100m mark at the global box office as it recorded the highest ever opening weekend figure for a non-music documentary in the UK.

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything earned an estimated $2.5m over the weekend on its sixth week of release in North America, according to Box Office Mojo, bringing its total there to $93.5m. This has been augmented by successful releases in a number of international territories, which has added an estimated $9m for a total of $102.5m.
